title: Text filters: wc, cut, sort, tr, sed & friends
about: What filters are and how they read standard input; counting, cutting, sorting, deduplicating, translating and editing text streams; comparing files.

questions.title: Definition of a filter
questions.text: What makes a command a "filter"?

options.t: It reads text from standard input or files, transforms it and writes the result to standard output, so it fits in a pipe.
It removes the files whose names match a pattern, and leaves the other files of the directory alone.
It works only on files given as arguments on the command line, and ignores whatever you type at the keyboard or send it in a pipe.
options.why: Most filters read standard input when no file is given.

options.t: It asks the user for confirmation before each change it makes, like an interactive installer.
options.why: Interactivity has nothing to do with it.

questions.title: Filter or not
questions.text: Does the command read text, transform it and write text, so that it fits in a pipeline?

items.why: Reads lines, writes them in a new order.
Selects columns of each line it reads.
Keeps only the lines that match.
An interactive editor; it does not produce a stream.
It acts on the file system and outputs nothing.
A builtin that changes the shell's state.

questions.title: No file given
questions.text: What does `wc -l` do when typed alone, with no file and no pipe?

options.t: It waits for input from the keyboard until you press `Ctrl+D`, then prints the number of lines typed.
options.why: With no operand, filters read standard input.

options.t: It fails at once with the error "missing file operand", since no file name was given.
options.why: Filters fall back to standard input instead.

options.t: It counts the lines of the listing of the current directory and prints the result, as if `ls` had been run before it.
It prints `0` straight away and exits, since there is nothing to count without a file.
options.why: It does not exit until it sees end of input.

questions.title: End of input
questions.text: To tell a filter reading from the keyboard that there is no more input, press `{{0}}`.
questions.note: `Ctrl+D` is not a signal: it makes the terminal report "end of file" to the program reading.

wrong.why: That sends `SIGINT` and kills the filter; any output it would have produced is lost.
That suspends the filter; it does not close its input.

questions.title: wc options
questions.text: Match each option of `wc` with what it counts.

pairs.why: Runs of spaces or tabs separate words.

pairs.r: Lines, words and bytes, in that order

questions.title: Lines of a file without newline
questions.text: `printf 'one two\nthree' | wc -l` prints 1, although the text seems to have two lines. Why?

options.t: `wc -l` counts newline characters, and the last line has none.
options.why: The text has one `\n`, so the answer is 1.

options.t: `wc -l` counts only those lines that have at least two words in them, and the last line has only one.
The first line is always ignored.
`printf` does not support `\n`.
options.why: It does, which is why one newline exists.

questions.title: wc with a file versus stdin
questions.text: How do the outputs of `wc -l data.txt` and `wc -l < data.txt` differ?

options.t: The first prints the count followed by the file name; the second prints only the count, because `wc` does not know the name.
options.why: Handy when a script needs just a number.

options.t: The second counts words instead of lines, because the redirection changes the meaning of `-l`.
The first counts the bytes of the file name, while the second counts the lines of the file.
options.why: It counts the lines of the file.

options.t: They are identical in every respect, since the shell passes the same file to `wc` in both cases and the output is the same.
options.why: The file name is shown only in the first.

questions.title: Count lines of a command
questions.text: Which pipeline prints how many entries are in the current directory (hidden ones excluded)?

options.t: `ls | wc -l`
options.why: `ls` prints one name per line when its output is a pipe.

options.t: `wc -l ls`
options.why: That would count the lines of a *file* called `ls`.

options.t: `ls -l | wc -w`
options.why: That counts words, including permissions and dates.

options.t: `ls > wc -l`
options.why: It would create a file named `wc` (with the `-l` as an argument of `ls`).

questions.title: Count three things
questions.text: What does `wc` print for the input `one two\nthree\n` (two lines, three words, 14 bytes)?

options.t: `2 3 14` (with padding)

options.why: The order is lines, words, bytes.

questions.title: cut by delimiter
questions.text: `cut -d: -f1,7 /etc/passwd` prints which parts of each line?

options.t: The first and the seventh fields of each line, separated by the colon.
options.why: `-d` is the delimiter and `-f` the field list.

options.t: The first and the seventh characters of each line, one after the other.
Lines number 1 and 7 of the file, printed complete and unchanged.
options.why: `cut` works within lines, not across them.

options.t: Everything in each line except fields 1 and 7, which are removed from it.

questions.title: cut field lists
questions.text: Match each option with the part of a colon-separated line it selects.

pairs.why: For example the user name in `/etc/passwd`.

pairs.r: The first and the seventh field

extras.why: `cut` does not filter lines by length.

questions.title: Default cut delimiter
questions.text: What is the default field delimiter of `cut -f2` when no `-d` is given?

options.t: The tab character.
options.why: Not a space: for blank-separated data use `-d' '` or `awk`.

options.t: A single space.
A comma.
Any run of white space.

questions.title: Lines without a delimiter
questions.text: What does `echo abc | cut -d: -f2` print?

options.t: `abc`: a line without the delimiter is printed unchanged, unless `-s` is given.
An empty line, because the second field does not exist in the input text and so there is nothing to print at all.
options.why: That is the output of `-f2` on a line that *has* the delimiter but an empty second field.

options.t: An error message saying that the delimiter was not found in the line.
`:abc`, with an empty second field added at the front of the line.

questions.title: Empty field
questions.text: What does `echo 'a,b,,d' | cut -d, -f3` print?

options.t: An empty line, because the third field is empty.
options.why: Consecutive delimiters make an empty field.

options.t: `d`, because `cut` skips the empty field and takes the next one.
options.why: `cut` does not skip the empty field.

options.t: `b`, which is the field that comes before the empty one.
An error message about the field, because it has no value.

questions.title: head and tail
questions.text: Match each command with the lines it prints from a 10-line input.

questions.title: Everything from line 6
questions.text: Print a file from its 6th line to the end: `tail -n {{0}} file`
questions.note: A plus sign means "starting at this line"; without it the number counts lines from the end.

wrong.why: That prints only the last 6 lines.
For `-n`, this is the same as 6: the last six lines.

questions.title: All but the first five
questions.text: Print every line except the first five: `tail -n {{0}} file`
questions.note: "Skip N lines" is "start at line N+1".

wrong.why: That starts at line 5, so the fifth line is still printed.
That prints the last five lines.

questions.title: Middle lines
questions.text: Which pipeline prints lines 4 to 7 of a file?

options.t: `head -n 7 file | tail -n 4`
options.why: The first seven lines, then the last four of those.

options.t: `head -n 4 file | tail -n 7`
options.why: That takes four lines, then asks for the last seven of them.

options.t: `tail -n 4 file | head -n 7`
options.why: That takes the last four lines of the file.

options.t: `cut -l 4-7 file`

questions.title: head -c
questions.text: What does `head -c 10 file` print?

options.t: The first 10 bytes of the file, not lines.
The first 10 lines of the file, as the option `-n 10` would print.
The count of the 10 lines, as a number printed on the screen.
The last 10 bytes of the file, which would need `tail -c 10`.

questions.title: tail -f
questions.text: What is `tail -f /var/log/syslog` used for?

options.t: To follow the file, printing new lines as they are appended, until you press `Ctrl+C`.
options.why: A standard way to watch logs live.

options.t: To print the first lines of the file and then stop, like `head` does, and to go on printing them until the end.
To find the word "f" in the file and print the lines that contain it.
To compress the file in the background while it keeps being written.

questions.title: Default sort order
questions.text: What order does plain `sort` use for the lines `b 10`, `a 9`, `c 100`?

options.t: Alphabetical by the whole line: `a 9`, `b 10`, `c 100`.
options.why: The default compares characters from the start of the line.

options.t: Numerical by the last number of each line, from the smallest to the largest.
The original order of the lines, since no option was given to `sort`.
By line length, with the shortest lines first and the longest ones last.

questions.title: Sorting numbers as text
questions.text: Given lines `a 9`, `b 10`, `c 100`, what does `sort -k2` (no `-n`) print first?

options.why: Text comparison: `10` and `100` start with `1`, which sorts before `9`.
That would be the result with `-n`.
`10` is shorter and sorts before `100` as text.

options.t: Nothing, `-k2` needs `-n`.

questions.title: sort options
questions.text: Match each option with its effect.

pairs.r: Sort by the third colon-separated field
Compare human-readable sizes such as 2K and 1G

extras.r: Sort in place, saving to the file

questions.title: Numeric descending by the second field
questions.text: Sort `data` by its second whitespace-separated field, numerically, largest first: `sort -k2 {{0}} {{1}} data`

wrong.why: That would sort in dictionary order (ignoring punctuation), not numerically.

questions.title: Top three
questions.text: Which command prints the three biggest numbers of a file with one number per line?

options.t: `sort -nr file | head -n 3`
options.why: Numerically in reverse, then the first three.

options.t: `sort file | head -n 3`
options.why: Those are the three smallest, in text order.

options.t: `head -n 3 file | sort`
options.why: Sorts only the first three lines of the file.

options.t: `tail -n 3 file`

questions.title: sort -u
questions.text: What is the difference between `sort -u file` and `uniq file` on an unsorted file?

options.t: `sort -u` sorts and removes all duplicates; `uniq` only merges duplicates that are next to each other.
options.why: That is why `uniq` is normally used after `sort`.

options.t: They are the same, because `uniq` also sorts its input before it removes the duplicate lines, so the two commands give one result.
options.why: On unsorted input, `uniq` leaves duplicates that are not adjacent.

options.t: `uniq` sorts the lines and `sort -u` does not, so the results differ only in their order.
`uniq` deletes the file it reads from and writes the unique lines into a new one.

questions.title: uniq options
questions.text: Match each command with its result on a sorted list.

pairs.why: A single copy of each line.

pairs.r: Prefix every line with its number of occurrences
Print only the lines that appear more than once
pairs.why: One copy of each repeated line.

pairs.r: Print only the lines that appear exactly once

questions.title: Word frequency
questions.text: Put the stages of a pipeline in order to list the most common words of a text, one per line, most frequent first.

items.why: Turn everything that is not a letter into line breaks: one word per line.
Identical words must become adjacent for `uniq`.
Count each run of identical words.
Order the counts from largest to smallest.

questions.title: Why sort before uniq
questions.text: Why does `uniq -c` usually come right after `sort` in a pipeline?

options.t: `uniq` only compares adjacent lines, so equal lines must be next to each other.
`uniq` refuses to start if its input is not sorted, and prints an error message.
options.why: It runs but gives misleading counts.

options.t: `sort` converts the text to numbers, which `uniq` needs in order to count them.
It is only a style convention, and the result is the same without `sort`.

questions.title: Predict uniq
questions.text: Given the lines `a`, `b`, `a` (in that order), what does `uniq` print?

options.t: All three lines: `a`, `b`, `a`
options.why: The two `a` lines are not adjacent.

options.t: `a` and `b`
options.why: That is the result of `sort -u` or `sort | uniq`.

options.t: `a` only
Nothing, the input is not sorted.

groups.title: Translating and editing: tr and sed

questions.title: What tr works on
questions.text: Which statement about `tr` is correct?

options.t: It works on characters of standard input; it cannot take file names as arguments.
It works on whole words, replacing each word of the first set by one of the second.
It only takes file names as arguments and never reads from standard input.
It edits the file in place, replacing the characters of the first set by the second.
options.why: It only writes to standard output.

questions.title: tr examples
questions.text: Match each `tr` command with its effect.

pairs.r: Convert lower case letters to upper case
pairs.why: Each character of the first set is replaced by its counterpart.

pairs.r: Squeeze runs of spaces into a single space

pairs.why: Often used to make columns readable.

questions.title: tr by positions
questions.text: What does `echo hello | tr el ip` print?

options.t: `hippo`
options.why: Each `e` becomes `i` and each `l` becomes `p`, by position in the two sets.

options.t: `hipio`
options.why: Both `l` become `p`; there is no `i` from a second `l`.

options.t: `ipllo`
options.why: That would replace the string `el` by `ip`.

options.t: `hello`

options.t: `Xaa`

`aXa`

pairs.r: Prints all lines except the second

questions.title: sed -n
questions.text: Why is `-n` used together with the `p` command in `sed -n '2p'`?

options.t: `-n` turns off the automatic printing of every line, so that only the lines selected by `p` appear.
options.why: Without it, line 2 would be printed twice.

options.t: `-n` makes `sed` edit the file itself in place, instead of writing the result of the substitution to the screen.
`-n` numbers the output lines, like the `nl` command does.
`-n` restricts `sed` to lines that contain numbers, skipping all the others.

questions.title: In-place editing
questions.text: Which option makes `sed` change the file itself rather than printing the result?

questions.title: Different delimiter
questions.text: Why is `sed 's#/usr#/opt#'` often written instead of using slashes?

options.t: Any character can separate the parts, and `#` avoids escaping the slashes in the paths.
options.why: `s/\/usr/\/opt/` means the same but is harder to read.

options.t: Because `#` makes the substitution global, so that every match on each line is replaced and not only the first one.
Because slashes are not allowed inside a `sed` command and would be rejected.
options.why: They are allowed; they just need escaping in the pattern.

options.t: Because `#` starts a comment, so the rest of the line is skipped by `sed`.

questions.title: Empty match surprise
questions.text: What does `echo hello | sed 's/l*/X/'` print?

options.t: `Xhello`
options.why: `l*` matches zero or more `l`; at the very start it matches the empty string, which is replaced by `X`.

options.t: `heXo`
`heXXo`
`hello`
options.why: There is a match, so it changes.

questions.title: Swap with groups
questions.text: What does `echo abc | sed 's/\(a\)\(b\)/\2\1/'` print?

options.t: `bac`
options.why: The groups captured `a` and `b`, and the replacement puts them back in reverse order.

options.t: `abc`
`cba`
options.why: Only the matched part `ab` is reversed.

questions.text: Remove all lines that contain `debug`: `sed '/debug/{{0}}' log`
questions.note: The address `/debug/` selects the lines; `d` deletes them.

wrong.why: That would print them twice (the default output plus `p`).
An incomplete substitute command that would be an error.

questions.title: Add a prefix
questions.text: What does `printf 'x\ny\n' | sed 's/^/> /'` produce?

options.t: The lines `> x` and `> y`
options.why: The anchor `^` matches the start of each line, where the text is inserted.

options.t: `> x` and `y`
`x> ` and `y> `
options.why: `^` is the start, not the end.

options.t: An error because `^` is reserved.

questions.title: tee
questions.text: In `make 2>&1 | tee build.log | grep error`, what does `tee` contribute?

options.t: It saves the complete output to `build.log` while still passing it on to `grep`.
options.why: You keep a full log and see the filtered view.

options.t: It discards the output that `grep` does not want, keeping only the error lines.
It runs the command `make` twice, once for the log and once for `grep`.
It replaces `grep`, since it also selects the lines that contain the word.

questions.title: tee -a
questions.text: Compared with `tee out.txt`, what does `tee -a out.txt` do differently?

options.t: It appends to the file instead of overwriting it.
It writes to all the files of the current directory at the same time.
It adds line numbers to the text that is passed through `tee`.
It suppresses the standard output, so that nothing appears on the screen.
options.why: Standard output still gets the data.

The position of the first differing byte

questions.title: diff status
questions.text: What exit status does `diff` return when the two files differ?

options.why: 0 means identical, 1 different, 2 trouble (for example a missing file).

questions.title: Reading a diff
questions.text: In the output of `diff old new`, a line starting with `<` means...

options.t: the line comes from the first file (`old`) and is missing or different in the second one.
options.why: `>` marks lines from the second file.

the line is identical in both files, which `diff` marks so that you can skip it.

questions.title: od purpose
questions.text: What is `od -c` (octal dump) useful for?

options.t: Showing the exact bytes of a file, including invisible ones such as tabs and newlines.
options.why: Good for debugging whitespace or binary data.

options.t: Converting numbers to octal inside a script, for example before a `chmod`.
Sorting the data of a file numerically, using the octal value of each byte as the key, so that the lines are in order.
Detecting duplicated files by comparing the octal dump of their contents.

questions.title: split
questions.text: What does `split -l 4 data part_` do to a 10-line file?

options.t: It writes `part_aa` and `part_ab` with 4 lines each and `part_ac` with the remaining 2.
It deletes every fourth line of the file and keeps the remaining lines in the files whose names start with `part_`.
It prints the first 4 lines of the file to the screen and then stops.
It creates 4 files of 10 lines each, repeating the lines of the input.
options.why: `-l 4` is lines per piece, not the number of pieces.

questions.title: Count users with bash
questions.text: Which pipeline counts the users of `/etc/passwd` whose login shell is `/bin/bash`?

options.t: `cut -d: -f7 /etc/passwd | grep -c '^/bin/bash$'`
options.why: The shell is field 7; `grep -c` counts the matching lines.

options.t: `cut -d: -f1 /etc/passwd | wc -l`, which counts all the users of the system, whatever shell they use
options.why: That counts all users, whatever their shell.

options.t: `cut -d: -f7 /etc/passwd | sort`, which only sorts the shells of the users without counting them
options.why: Sorts the shells but does not count.

options.t: `wc -l /bin/bash`, which counts the lines of the program file of the shell itself
options.why: Counts the lines of the program file.

questions.title: Users in order
questions.text: Which pipeline prints the login names of all users, sorted alphabetically?

options.t: `cut -d: -f1 /etc/passwd | sort`
`sort | cut -d: -f1 /etc/passwd`
options.why: `sort` would read the keyboard, and the file is given to `cut` only.

options.t: `cut -d: -f7 /etc/passwd | sort`
`sort -d /etc/passwd`
options.why: Sorts whole lines in dictionary order.

questions.title: Name and home with a tab
questions.text: Which pipeline prints each user name and home directory separated by a tab?

options.t: `cut -d: -f1,6 /etc/passwd | tr ':' '\t'`
options.why: The fields are taken first, then the colon is translated to a tab.

options.t: `cut -d: -f1,6 /etc/passwd | tr '\t' ':'`
`tr ':' '\t' | cut -f1,6 /etc/passwd`
`cut -f1,6 /etc/passwd`
options.why: The default delimiter is a tab, not a colon.

questions.title: Longest line
questions.text: Which command prints the length of the longest line of a file?

options.t: `wc -L file`
options.why: The capital `-L` reports the maximum line length (and `wc -l` with a lowercase L the number of lines).

options.t: `wc -l file`
options.why: Counts lines, not characters per line.

options.t: `sort file | tail -n 1`
options.why: Gives the alphabetically last line, which is not necessarily the longest.

options.t: `cut -c1 file`
options.why: Prints only the first character of every line.

questions.title: Order of filters
questions.text: What is wrong with `sort -n data | head -n 3` when you want the three *largest* numbers?

options.t: `sort -n` orders from smallest to largest, so `head` gives the three smallest; add `-r`.
Nothing is wrong with the command: it is correct as it stands, and it prints the three largest numbers of the file.
`head` cannot read from a pipe, so it would wait for the keyboard instead.
The option `-n` does not work with `sort`, it is only valid for `head`.
options.why: It is an option of `sort` here.

questions.title: Words in a file
questions.text: `echo "the cat the dog" | tr ' ' '\n' | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head -n 1` prints which line?

options.why: One word per line, sorted, counted, with the most frequent first.

options.t: `1 cat`, because the pipeline lists the words in alphabetical order
options.why: `the` appears twice, which is the highest count.

options.t: `4 the cat the dog`, because the line is counted as a whole
options.why: The line is split into words first.

options.t: `the`, because `uniq -c` prints only the repeated word
